0.title: API
0.text:
seo(options?)
The Vite plugin. Returns a Vite Plugin (gasp, i know, how shocking).
import { seo } from "vite-plugin-seo-meta";

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [seo({ site: { url: "https://example.com", name: "My Site" } })],
});

Options



Option
Type
Default
Notes




site
SiteConfig
-
Site defaults


pages
Record<string, PageMeta>
{}
Per-page overrides


robots
"auto" | boolean | RobotsFileOptions
"auto"
false disables generation


sitemap
"auto" | boolean | SitemapOptions
"auto"
false disables generation


validate
"warn" | "error" | false
"warn"
Validation policy


configFile
string | false
"seo.config.ts"
Path to config file, or false to skip auto-detection



defineSeoConfig(config)
A typed identity function that returns its argument unchanged. This only exists so that the config can be easily typechecked.
import { defineSeoConfig } from "vite-plugin-seo-meta";

export default defineSeoConfig({
  site: { url: "https://example.com", name: "My Site" },
  pages: { "/about": { title: "About" } },
});

The plugin auto-detects seo.config.ts in the project root and loads it. Set configFile: false to disable this.
applySeo(page, site?)
Runtime helper for SPAs. Updates managed head elements after a route change.
import { applySeo } from "vite-plugin-seo-meta/runtime";

applySeo({ title: "New Page", description: "..." });

See SPA Runtime. (No, no, not a spa, a Single-Page Application, though we all would love that… probably.)
Exported types
The plugin exports types for every config shape:

SeoPluginOptions - options accepted by seo()
SeoOptions - the full beeg config (site, pages, robots, sitemap, validate)
SiteConfig - site defaults
PageMeta - per-page overrides
OpenGraphInfo - Open Graph values
TwitterInfo - Twitter Card values
FaviconConfig - favicon and platform icons
RobotsFileOptions - robots.txt options
RobotsGroup - an RFC 9309 agent group
SitemapOptions - sitemap options
ImageRef / ImageInput - image references, including thumbnail for video sitemaps
JsonLdConfig - JSON-LD configuration
HreflangAlternate - a hreflang entry
ThemeColorEntry - a theme color meta tag
TwitterCardType - summary | summary_large_image | player | app
TwitterHandle - a Twitter @handle
TwitterAppPlatform - iphone | ipad | googleplay
TwitterPlayer - player card iframe config
TwitterApps - app card per-platform config
ArticleJsonLd / OrganizationJsonLd / WebSiteJsonLd / ProductJsonLd / JsonLdPerson - JSON-LD shapes
OpenGraphArticle / OpenGraphBook / OpenGraphMusic / OpenGraphVideo / OpenGraphPayment - Open Graph verticals
SitemapChangefreq - changefreq enum
RobotsDirectives - structured robots meta directives

6.title: Configuration
6.text:
Everything lives under a site chunk, but per-page overrides go in pages.
The plugin fills in defaults for anything you leave out.
site



Field
Type
Default
Notes




url
string
required
Site URL, must be absolute. Used as the canonical base and og:url


name
string
required
Site name


title
string
name
Used when a page does not set its own


titleTemplate
string
%s | name
%s is replaced with the page title


description
string
required
Page description fallback


locale
string
en_US
og:locale


author
string
-
author meta tag


image
string
-
Default og:image


twitter
object
-
See Twitter Cards


favicon
object
-
See Favicon & platform icons


jsonLd
object
-
See JSON-LD



pages
A map of route to page configurations, of which routes are matched against the built HTML filename.
pages: {
  "/": { title: "Home" },
  "/about": { title: "About", description: "About us" },
  "/blog/post-slug": { title: "Post", noindex: true },
}

Per-page fields



Field
Type
Notes




title
string
Overrides site.title


description
string
Overrides site.description


canonical
string
Absolute URL. Defaults to site.url + route


noindex
boolean
Adds noindex. Excludes from sitemap


robots
string|string[]
Merged into the robots meta tag


alternates
array
See hreflang


openGraph
object
See Open Graph


jsonLd
object
See JSON-LD


image
string
Page-specific og:image


twitter
object
Page-specific Twitter overrides



robots
robots can be false (skip generation), an array of rules, or a config object.
robots: {
  userAgent: "*",
  disallow: ["/api", "*.gif$"],
  allow: ["/public"],
  crawlDelay: 5,
  cleanParam: ["sessionid"],
  host: "example.com",
  sitemap: "https://example.com/sitemap.xml",
  disallowNoindex: true,
  groups: [
    { userAgent: "GoogleBot", disallow: ["/private"] },
  ],
}


merge (default true): preserve existing public/robots.txt, append generated rules, drop duplicates
disallowNoindex (default false): also emit Disallow for pages with noindex: true
groups: following the RFC 9309 agent groups, each with their own userAgent, disallow, allow, crawlDelay, cleanParam

sitemap
sitemap: {
  exclude: ["/admin"],
  maxUrls: 100_000,
  defaultChangefreq: "weekly",
  defaultPriority: 0.8,
  siteUrl: "https://example.com",
}


maxUrls (default 50000): URL cap. Sitemaps split into multiple files past this
Image, video and news namespaces are emitted automatically when a page has matching openGraph data
xhtml:link alternates are emitted for pages with hreflang companions

validation



Value
Behavior




"warn"
Log issues (default)


"error"
Throw, fails the build


false
Disable



The plugin checks include enums (changefreq, twitter.card), required fields, absolute URLs, length budgets (title 60, description 50-160, Twitter 70/200), duplicate titles and canonicals, and conflicting noindex/sitemap settings, all typical stuff.
Coexistence
If vite-plugin-sitemap, vite-plugin-pwa or other detected plugins are present, this plugin warns and bails on generating sitemap.xml and robots.txt unless you explicitly enable them: sitemap: true, robots: true.

14.title: Installation
14.text:
Install the plugin (It (obviously) needs Vite as a peer dependency).
npm i -D vite-plugin-seo-meta vite

Vite 5 or newer is required.
The plugin is ESM only. If your project is CommonJS, switch to ESM (easier said than done, to be fair) or use the .cjs build.
Build output
The plugin builds to dist/index.js (ESM) and dist/index.cjs (CommonJS). The runtime helper is a separate entry (as why would you want to compile a vite-plugin for web, and vice versa):
import { applySeo } from "vite-plugin-seo-meta/runtime";

Importing the runtime pulls in the client-side navigation handler. It is tree-shaken (aka, yeeted) out of the main build if you do not use it.

19.title: hreflang
19.text:
hreflang alternates are emitted as <link rel="alternate"> tags. They live in pages[].alternates.
pages: {
  "/": {
    alternates: [
      { hreflang: "en", href: "https://example.com/" },
      { hreflang: "es", href: "https://example.com/es/" },
      { hreflang: "x-default", href: "https://example.com/" },
    ],
  },
}


What each field means

hreflang: the language or region code. Use ISO 639-1 for languages, or en-US, es-MX for language-region pairs. Region codes come from ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 which are the two-letter country codes
href: the absolute URL of that variant
x-default: a catch-all for searchers who do not match any listed language or region. Point it at your default page

Rules

Every href must be an absolute URL
The page should list itself in its own alternates. If the page is the English variant, include { hreflang: "en", href: "https://example.com/" }
The plugin emits xhtml:link alternates in sitemap.xml for pages that have hreflang companions
hreflang URLs must all resolve to the same host. The sitemap enforces this.

Big “Don’t Do This”
Listing a variant that does not exist. If you say es points to https://example.com/es/ and that page is a 404, search engines will show the error to Spanish users. So, obviously, don’t mess up your deployments.
When to use it

You have the same content in multiple languages
You have the same content for different regions (.com, .com.au, .ca)
You want to tell search engines which variant to show which user

If you do not have multiple languages, leave alternates out. The plugin does not add anything on its own (yet? maybe.)

24.title: JSON-LD

32.title: Meta Tags
32.text:
The plugin emits standard meta tags (<meta> tags) for every page. You set the defaults in site and override per page in pages.
title
The <title> comes from the page title, falling back to site.title. The titleTemplate wraps it.
You can pass a string or a function to titleTemplate. The string should contain %s where the page title should go. The function receives the page title and returns a string, for example:
site: {
  title: "My Site",
  titleTemplate: "%s | My Site",
},
pages: { "/about": { title: "About Us" } },

Renders as <title>About Us | My Site</title>.
Keep titles under 60 characters. The validator enforces this, and it’s generally a good idea to follow it: titles that are too long may be truncated in search results… and that’s bad.
description
The <meta name="description"> comes from the page description, falling back to site.description.
site: { description: "My awesome site" },
pages: { "/about": { description: "Who we are and what we build." } },

Keep descriptions between 50 and 160 characters. Also enforced.
canonical
<link rel="canonical"> points to the page URL. It defaults to site.url + route. Set it explicitly when the same content lives at multiple URLs.
pages: {
  "/product": { canonical: "https://example.com/products/widget" },
}

Canonicals must be absolute URLs. The validator checks this. Google’s guidance on canonicals is available here and it’s worth reading if you’re ever unsure whether to set one!
robots meta
Per-page robots adds a <meta name="robots"> value. It does not touch robots.txt, which is generated separately.
The valid directives are documented in Google’s robots meta tag reference. The plugin accepts all of them!
pages: { "/private": { robots: "noindex, nofollow" } }

noindex: true is shorthand for robots: "noindex". It also (obviously)excludes the page from sitemap.xml.
noindex and crawling
A page with noindex: true tells crawlers not to index it, but by default it does not add a Disallow rule to robots.txt. Crawlers can still reach the page to see the noindex directive. This is done because some crawlers (like Googlebot) still index pages… even if they’re marked noindex, cause Google just do be like that sometimes.
To block crawling outright, set disallowNoindex: true on the robots config:
robots: {
  disallowNoindex: true;
}

Favicon and platform icons (subject to change)
The favicon block emits link tags and meta tags for browsers and platforms:
site: {
  favicon: {
    icon: "/favicon.ico",
    appleTouchIcon: "/apple-touch-icon.png",
    appleTouchIconPrecomposed: "/apple-touch-icon-precomposed.png",
    manifest: "/manifest.json",
    maskIcon: "/mask-icon.svg",
    maskIconColor: "#000000",
    mobileWebApp: {
      title: "My App",
      capable: true,
      statusBarStyle: "black-translucent",
    },
    msapplication: {
      tileColor: "#ffffff",
      tileImage: "/tile.png",
      config: "/browserconfig.xml",
    },
  },
}


maskIconColor defaults to #000000
mobileWebApp covers apple-mobile-web-app-title, apple-mobile-web-app-capable and apple-mobile-web-app-status-bar-style
msapplication covers msapplication-TileColor, msapplication-TileImage and msapplication-config

I plan to eventually fold this into the main seo block and automatically fill in the various fields and manifest and browserconfig files from the existing data, and also generate all icons from a single source image. For now, you have to provide all of these manually.

49.title: robots.txt
49.text:
RFC 9309 defines the robots.txt standard. Originally made by Martijn Koster in 1994 (the original spec), because robots kept crawling sites and causing a ruckus. (Seems mighty familiar to today’s AI bots, doesn’t it?) The standard has been (barely) updated over the years, and this plugin implements the latest version.

It’s generated at build time. It can be disabled, replaced, or merged with an existing file.
Basic rules
robots: {
  userAgent: "*",
  disallow: ["/api", "*.gif$"],
  allow: ["/public"],
  crawlDelay: 5,
  cleanParam: ["sessionid"],
  host: "example.com",
  sitemap: "https://example.com/sitemap.xml",
  disallowNoindex: true,
}


userAgent: who the rules apply to. Default *
disallow: paths to block. Supports * (match anything) and $ (end of string)
allow: paths to explicitly permit, overriding disallow
crawlDelay: delay in seconds
cleanParam: URL parameters to ignore when crawling
host: the Host: record
sitemap: URL to advertise, or false to omit. Defaults to site.url + /sitemap.xml
disallowNoindex: also block pages with noindex: true

Wildcards
* matches any sequence of characters. $ matches the end of the URL.
disallow: ["/api", "*.gif$", "/private/*"];


/api blocks /api, /api/foo, /api/foo/bar (basically anything under it)
*.gif$ blocks /img/cat.gif but not /img/cat.png (which… is obviously not a GIF)
/private/* blocks everything under /private (also /private/foo, /private/foo/bar, etc.) but not /private itself. Use /private to block that too.

allow takes priority when a path matches both. So allow: ["/public"] lets crawlers through even if disallow: ["/"].
Agent groups
Different crawlers get different rules:
robots: {
  groups: [
    {
      userAgent: "GoogleBot",
      disallow: ["/private"],
      crawlDelay: 2,
    },
    {
      userAgent: "BingBot",
      allow: ["/"],
    },
  ],
}

Each group has its own userAgent, disallow, allow, crawlDelay and cleanParam. The default group (top-level fields) applies to *.
Merge with an existing file
By default the plugin preserves robots.txt in the output directory and appends generated rules. Duplicates are dropped.
To overwrite instead, set merge: false:
robots: {
  merge: false;
}

noindex and crawling
A page with noindex: true tells crawlers not to index it. By default it does not add a Disallow rule, so crawlers can still reach the page to see the directive.
To block crawling outright:
robots: {
  disallowNoindex: true;
}

Raw lines
Append literal lines after the generated rules:
robots: {
  rules: [
    "User-agent: *",
    "Disallow: /",
  ],
}

Use this when the plugin does not cover something. The lines are emitted verbatim.

70.title: Twitter Cards
70.text:
Twitter Cards control how a link looks on Twitter (i’m not calling it X). They live in the twitter block, which inherits from site.twitter.
site: {
  twitter: {
    site: "@Twitter",
    creator: "@Twitter",
  },
}



Side note: X decided to delete all their documentation, so I had to find them in the Wayback Machine, which was tedium.

Card types



Value
Use case




summary
Small card with thumbnail


summary_large_image
Large image card


player
Embedded video or audio player


app
Promote an app



Basic fields
twitter: {
  card: "summary_large_image",
  site: "@mysite",
  creator: "@alice",
  title: "Hello, world",
  description: "My first post on this site.",
  image: "https://example.com/card.png",
  imageAlt: "A screenshot of the post",
  imageWidth: 1200,
  imageHeight: 630,
}


site and creator are @handles
imageAlt is required when image is set. Max 420 characters
imageWidth and imageHeight are the card image dimensions in pixels

Numeric IDs
Instead of @handles, use numeric IDs:
twitter: {
  siteId: "1234567890",
  creatorId: "0987654321",
}

siteId replaces site. creatorId replaces creator. Use whichever you have.
Label and data pairs
Summary cards can carry two label/value pairs:
twitter: {
  card: "summary",
  label1: "Price",
  data1: "$199",
  label2: "Stock",
  data2: "In stock",
}

Player Card
For embedded video or audio:
twitter: {
  card: "player",
  player: {
    url: "https://example.com/player.html",
    width: 1280,
    height: 720,
    stream: "https://example.com/stream.mp4",
  },
}


url is the HTTPS iframe URL.
width and height are the iframe dimensions in pixels.
stream is optional. It points to a raw video or audio stream.

App Card
Promote an app. One entry per platform:
twitter: {
  card: "app",
  apps: {
    iphone: { name: "My App", id: "1234567890", url: "myapp://open" },
    ipad: { name: "My App", id: "1234567890", url: "myapp://open" },
    googleplay: { name: "My App", id: "com.example.myapp", url: "myapp://open" },
  },
  country: "US",
}


name is the app name (who knew)
id is the app store ID
url is a custom URL scheme. It must include ://. You also have to register the scheme in your app. See Apple and Google for details.
country is the two-letter ISO country code for the App Store that holds the app.

74.title: Twitter Cards > Label and data pairs

77.title: Validation
77.text:
The plugin validates config at build time. By default it logs issues and continues. Set validate: "error" to fail the build. I’d recommend doing this in CI, so you catch problems before they reach production!!!
seo({ validate: "error" });

Modes



Value
Behavior




"warn"
Log issues (default)


"error"
Throw, fails the build


false
Disable



What it checks
Enums

changefreq must be one of always, hourly, daily, weekly, monthly, yearly, never
twitter.card must be one of summary, summary_large_image, player, app

Required fields

site.url must be set
site.name and site.description are required when their page-level values are missing

Absolute URLs
Canonicals, og:url, twitter:image and twitter:player URLs must be absolute. Relative URLs are resolved against site.url before validation, so this check runs on the resolved value.
Length budgets



Field
Limit




title
60 characters


description
50-160 characters


twitter:title
70 characters


twitter:description
200 characters


twitter:image:alt
420 characters



Duplicates

Two pages with the same title
Two pages with the same canonical

Conflicts

A page with noindex: true that is also in sitemap.xml (noindex pages are excluded from the sitemap by default, but this catches explicit overrides, juuuust in case)
A page with sitemap: false that still has hreflang alternates

How to fix
The validator reports the field, the route, and the problem. Fix the field and rebuild. It does not guess what you meant… because well… it shouldn’t; the SEO checks here are strict. If you want to disable a check, set validate: false or remove the field entirely.

87.title: vite-plugin-seo-meta
87.text:
vite-plugin-seo-meta
Serverless SEO for Vite. One plugin generates <title>, meta tags, canonical URLs, Open Graph, Twitter Cards, JSON-LD, hreflang, robots.txt and sitemap.xml. Zero-config defaults, per-page overrides. Works for SPA, MPA, SSG and prerendered builds.
Vite
SEO
TypeScript


  

Quick Start


  
  
  

Live Demo
GitHub

// vite.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from "vite";
import { seo } from "vite-plugin-seo-meta";

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [
    seo({
      site: {
        url: "https://example.com",
        name: "My Site",
        title: "My Site",
        titleTemplate: "%s | My Site",
        description: "My awesome site",
      },
    }),
  ],
});




Why this plugin
Writing SEO by hand means repeating the same tags for every page, keeping them in sync when the site changes, and forgetting a field on the one page you forget at 3 AM, or deleting mysterious ones that keep your site up top on Google. So… this plugin generates them from a single config and per-page overrides, so the tags are always consistent.
It also handles the files that are très important:

robots.txt follows RFC 9309 and happens to support agent groups, Allow/Disallow wildcards and Crawl-delay
sitemap.xml supports image, video and news namespaces with single-host enforcement and a URL capacity (extensible)
Twitter Cards have the typical summary, player and app cards with :site:id and :creator:id variants
Favicon and platform icons cover apple-touch-icon, mask-icon, mobile web app and msapplication tags

What it does not do
This plugin does not generate social images or app icons (very big Yet). That is a future thing I plan to add hehe.
